title: memory-fragmentation-lit-scraps-rina-kapoor
content:
Purpose / quick summary:
I sketched a lightweight reading list and experiment skeleton around what I'm calling \"memory fragmentation\" in KV-style caches for autoregressive inference. Goal: practical ideas we can try on Redwood serving runtime to reduce memory footprint and tail latency when many short, interleaved sessions share the same model instance or cache shard.

Context / motivation:
- In our Dedicated/Private deployments we observe many concurrent short chats where each session has tiny prefixes. That leads to lots of small KV entries with low reuse but high metadata overhead.
- Papers on KV compression and memory-efficient attention propose various encodings; the systems-level cost/benefit tradeoffs for production inference (latency + cost) aren't well explored.
- Want to prioritize changes that are low-risk operationally (no model retrain) and that can be toggled per-customer or per-pool.

Key papers / takeaways (very quick, informal):
1) \"Compact KV Encodings for Transformer Caches\" (hypothetical summary of related work) - shows simple PCA / product quantization on keys reduces memory, but lookup noise grows. Important: quantize only for cold segments, keep recent keys exact.
2) Recurrent-memory / compressed attention notes (ICLR/NeurIPS-style) - compress sequences into summaries (low-rank) when they cross a length threshold; can be decoded back to approx keys. Good when long histories are mostly redundant.
3) Eviction & TTL strategies (systems papers) - LRU alone is poor with many short sessions; time-based TTL per-session or per-prefix-length performs better for throughput.

Open questions from reading:
- How sensitive are decoding logits to approximate keys? If some small drift is acceptable, we can aggressively compress older prefixes. But need to measure hallucination/quality impact across prompt types (fact QA vs creative chat).
- Is per-customer policy feasible to implement in routing/placement layer? We can tag requests with caching policy metadata but will add overhead.

Experiment ideas to run on Redwood infra (ordered by cost to implement):
A) Offline simulation harness (low cost)
  - Replay recent request traces (anonymized) and simulate different eviction/compaction policies. Metrics: cache hit rate, average stored KB per session, simulated per-token CPU/GPU memory pressure, estimate cost impact.
  - Output: show candidate policies that reduce memory by X% with <Y% drop in simulated quality (using stored logits or generation proxies).

B) Canary runtime: TTL + proactive compaction (medium cost)
  - Implement TTL buckets (e.g., 30s, 5m, 1h) and a background compaction that consolidates small contiguous KV segments into a single compressed chunk once older than X seconds.
  - Measure: tail memory, p95/p99 latency impact, throughput. Also check generation divergence on canonical eval prompts.

C) Quantized-cold-store (higher cost)
  - Cold segments (not referenced in last N tokens) get moved to a quantized storage layer (PQ or 8-bit). When accessed, do a cheap approximate lookup and optionally decompress on hot access.
  - Measure: access latency for cold->hot transition, cost savings, and quality delta on downstream tokens.

D) Session grouping heuristics for continuous batching (experimental)
  - Group requests by recent prefix similarity to increase re-use and reduce fragmentation. Could use a simple hash of last k tokens or a tiny sketch.

Metrics / evaluation plan:
- Memory metrics: peak GPU/host memory attributed to KV per-pool, average per-session stored bytes, number of cache objects.
- Latency/cost: p50/p95/p99 token generation latency, throughput, GPU utilization.
- Quality: automatic evals (perplexity on held-out prompts), human-labeled sample set for hallucination/answer correctness (~50 prompts per policy). Also a small A/B on live traffic if safe.

Practical constraints and risks:
- Any strategy that changes exact KV keys risks subtle quality regressions. We should prefer reversible or on-access decompressible formats for initial canaries.
- Background compaction must not spike latency during on-demand decompression. Use rate limiters and cap background I/O.
- Per-customer policies may complicate autoscaling decisions (different memory-density workloads).

Notes-to-self / TODOs:
- Get anonymized trace sample from prod (talk to SRE: JIRA-PLAT-4821). Need: per-request token counts, session IDs (hashed), timestamps, model variant, pool id.
- Build replay harness that can simulate TTL/eviction (priority #1). Talk to Devin (mosaic-cache experiments) for replay tooling pointers.
- Design minimal metrics dashboard: cache size by TTL bucket, compaction ops/sec, decompress latency distribution. Work with observability to add tags.
- Quick sanity check: try rough PQ on a small toy cache (GPT-2 sized) in a notebook, measure cosine similarity of queries to compressed keys.

Brainstorm of low-effort heuristics to test quickly:
- Merge contiguous short sessions from same user/IP into a single cache namespace for short time window (reduces small-object overhead).
- Prefer time-based eviction instead of LRU for sessions under N tokens.
- Aggressive quantize older than 10 minutes, but keep last 2 segments exact.

Questions for the team:
- Is there appetite from Dedicated/Private customers to accept slightly lossy caches in exchange for lower bills? Could be an opt-in premium feature.
- Any prior infra work for background compaction that I should reuse? (maybe platform-engineering has similar for logs).

References / bookmarks:
- Placeholder arXiv and conference links here for follow-up.
- Related internal docs: JIRA-PLAT-4821 (trace export), CONFLUENCE: Cache-cost-model-draft (ask observability).

Final note (quick):
This feels like a promising area to get concrete wins: low-hanging systems improvements that reduce memory and cost without touching model weights. Prioritize building a replay harness and a cost/quality ROI calculator before any runtime changes.

Scratch/stream-of-consciousness fragments:
- \"compress older prefixes into 1 summary vector\" vs \"PQ each key individually\" — which degrades generation less?
- Might combine with routing: route suspiciously long/low-value sessions to a lower-memory pool with more aggressive compaction.
- If compacted keys introduce bias, could add small calibration pass on generation start (cheap).

-- Rina
